Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Describe the classification system for bunionette deformity.
List nonsurgical treatment options for management of a symptomatic bunionette.
Describe three general surgical treatment options for the management of bunionette
deformity and the indications for each option.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
A bunionette deformity, or a tailor bunion, is a prominence of the lateral aspect of the fifth
metatarsal head.

Epidemiology
A female-to-male ratio ranging from 3:1 to 10:1 has been reported in series on symptomatic
bunionette deformity.1
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Three main bony anatomic variations result in bunionette deformity.
Enlarged fifth metatarsal head
Increased lateral deviation of the fifth metatarsal
Widening of the fourth and fifth metatarsal intermetatarsal angle (IMA)
Associated bursitis is common, as is callosity at the lateral and/or plantar aspect of the fifth
metatarsal head.
Etiology
Anatomic variations in shape and alignment of fifth metatarsal
Constrictive shoe wear
Association with pes planus
Natural History
Many patients with bunionette deformity are asymptomatic.
Deformity generally is static.
Associated bursitis may vary depending on activity or inflammatory conditions.

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Clinical Presentation
Clinical presentation consists of pain and bursa formation resulting from painful rubbing of
the prominence against the lateral counter of a shoe.
Imaging Studies
Weight-bearing AP radiographs should be obtained.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Initial nonsurgical management involves wearing properly fitting shoes with a wider toe box
and padding of the lateral prominence.
Surgical Management
Indications
Whether surgical management is necessary depends on the type of bunionette deformity;
however, surgical management rarely is necessary.
Type 1
Lateral condylectomy with reefing of the lateral metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint capsule
If the deformity is large and long-standing, combining the lateral condylectomy with a distal
metatarsal chevron-medializing osteotomy is indicated.
Type 2 and type 3
If the IMA is less than 12° or a small lateral curvature of the fifth metatarsal is present, a
distal chevron osteotomy can be performed. A maximum medializing translation of 2 to 3
mm is recommended with a chevron osteotomy; a larger amount of medial translation may
result in an unstable osteotomy. A 2-mm mini fragment screw is recommended for fixation;
however, Kirschner wires or bioabsorbable pins are alternatives.
A distal metatarsal oblique osteotomy (Kramer or minimally invasive style) can be performed.
This osteotomy requires less soft-tissue disruption and does not necessitate a condylectomy
or capsular reefing. The osteotomy allows for a greater shift and correction and is fixed with

the use of an axial Kirschner wire. Therefore, this oblique osteotomy can be used to manage
wider IMA deformities. Although the osteotomy is less intrinsically stable, healing and results
are good.2-4
An oblique diaphyseal rotational osteotomy with screw fixation is used in patients with a larger
bunionette deformity who have an IMA greater than 12° or a large fifth metatarsal lateral
curvature. Metatarsal head resection results in unacceptable instability of the MTP joint and
should be reserved for salvage procedures.
Proximal metatarsal osteotomy is associated with a relatively high rate of nonunion because of
disruption of the vascular supply of the proximal fifth metatarsal.
Contraindications
Poor skin quality
Inadequate vascular arterial flow
Complications
Recurrence of deformity
Most common with lateral condylectomy alone
Transfer metatarsalgia
Most common with fifth metatarsal head resection
Nonunion
Most common with proximal fifth metatarsal osteotomy
Valgus instability of the fifth MTP joint
Caused by excessive lateral condylectomy
Medial subluxation of the fifth MTP joint
Adequate lateral capsule reconstruction helps decrease risk.
Infection
Displacement of the osteotomy
Common if osteotomy is performed without internal or percutaneous fixation
Digital nerve injury
Osteonecrosis of metatarsal head
An oblique diaphyseal rotational osteotomy with screw fixation is used in patients with a larger
bunionette deformity who have an IMA greater than 12° or a large fifth metatarsal lateral

curvature. Metatarsal head resection results in unacceptable instability of the MTP joint and

Outcomes
Kitaoka and Holiday5,6 reported on lateral condylectomy in 21 feet (16 patients), with 71% of
patients satisfied with their results. Radiographic angular correction was minimal. The
technique was unable to manage plantar keratosis.
Kitaoka et al7 reported on distal chevron osteotomy in 19 feet (13 patients), with 63% having
good or excellent results. Internal or percutaneous fixation was not routinely performed.
Boyer and Deorio8 reported on distal chevron osteotomy with bioabsorbable pin fixation in 12
feet (10 patients). All osteotomies healed by 6 weeks postoperatively. The mean postoperative
American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society score was 93 out of 100, and all patients were
satisfied with the procedure.
Coughlin9,10 reported on diaphyseal osteotomy with internal fixation, distal lateral
condylectomy, and soft-tissue repair in 30 feet (20 patients). At a mean follow-up of 31
months, 93% had good or excellent results. The mean IMA improved from 16° to 0.5°. One
delayed union was reported.
Lee et al4 reported on 38 patients (43 feet) treated via a modified Kramer osteotomy fixed with
the use of a percutaneous Kirschner wire for 2 weeks, with a mean follow-up of 55 months.
The mean postoperative Foot Function Index was 19.4. The mean fourth and fifth metatarsal
IMA and the mean fifth MTP angle improved. Results included five delayed unions and one
nonunion, which did not require management. All patients with a diagnosis of delayed union
or nonunion were asymptomatic.
Lewis et al11 performed a systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 studies (714 feet in 580
patients) on bunionette deformity correction via percutaneous or minimally invasive
osteotomy techniques. Most of studies did not use any internal or percutaneous fixation for
the osteotomy. Complication rates ranged from zero to 21.4%, and nonunion rates ranged
from zero to 5.6%.
